node.label: Lauren Benton
node.date_label: Colonial Law and Cultural Difference (1999) · Law and Colonial Cultures (edition imprint 2002) · A Search for Sovereignty (edition imprint 2010) · Humanity interview (2011) · with Richard J. Ross, Legal Pluralism and Empires (2013)
node.description: Studies jurisdictional conflicts, colonial legal practices and the uneven reach of imperial sovereignty. Her early book introduction connects repeated local legal contests with broader patterns of world history. A Search for Sovereignty examines how delegated authority and mobile subjects helped produce corridors, enclaves and differentiated legal spaces. In a later interview she argues that legal authorization could enable imperial violence even where authority was fragmented. The selected readings expose her historical questions and methodological distinctions; they do not make one account of legal pluralism binding on every empire.

node.scope_note: Selected legal-historical writings and first-person explanations, with later scholarship dated explicitly. Neither a full career review nor whole-book reading is claimed. Read Law and Colonial Cultures chapter 1 pp. 1–10; A Search for Sovereignty pp. 1–5 and 7–10 plus preface xi–xii; selected Benton answers in the 2011 Humanity interview pp. 75–76, 78–79 and 82–83. Original case records, later book chapters, the 1999 article body and the 2013 collection remain unread. The two copyright leaves explicitly state first publication 2002 and 2010, while Core lists earlier print-release dates 2001 and 2009; source notes preserve both observations. Dan Edelstein’s claims are not attributed to Benton. The postcolonial-history connection is a contextual contribution on colonial legal categories, not adherence to every postcolonial theory. Stern’s 2011 book is a separate, unread comparative resource, not evidence of influence. No lifespan, continuous career interval or review-through year is assigned.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses repeated jurisdictional conflicts and legal routines to connect local colonial encounters with institutional patterns in world history (Law and Colonial Cultures, 2002 imprint).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own introduction pp. 3–7 read, especially the move from multiple legal authorities to institutional world history. A particular comparative research strategy is being added; neither a founding of global history nor uniform legal development across all regions is asserted. The argument is not inferred from the dissertation citation count.

incident_edges.relationship: Makes conflicts over legal forums, cultural difference and intermediaries part of explaining colonial authority, with divisions among colonizers and among colonized populations (2002 imprint).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own introduction pp. 1–3 and 8–10 read. Jurisdictional disputes are multisided; state authority is treated as historically produced through contests over law rather than a finished apparatus imposed intact. This is a contextual contribution to colonial/postcolonial historical inquiry, not a claim that Benton endorses a shared postcolonial doctrine or that legal strategies guaranteed emancipation.

incident_edges.relationship: Reconstructs imperial space through legal corridors, enclaves and delegated authority rather than assuming even territorial sovereignty (A Search for Sovereignty, 2010 imprint; interview 2011).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 2–5 and 7–9 and preface xi–xii read; Benton’s interview answers pp. 75–76 and 82–83 explain the relation between legal practices, spatial patterns and authorized violence. Uneven authority is her historical argument, not proof that every empire lacked territorial ambitions. The nineteenth-century changes and the limits of extending the analogy to present situations remain explicit in her final answer.

named_group_routes.relationship: Explains a global method that relates merchants, plantations and manufacturing across regions, treating capitalism as connected diversity rather than a single preordained path (GrowthPolicy interview, 2020).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Beckert’s second answer was read: comparative regional sites and linked labour regimes support this account of his method. A first-person research strategy does not establish universal adoption, prove every regional empirical claim, or derive a new argument from the unread 2025 book. The field’s prior approaches, Benton addition and review boundary remain intact.

named_group_routes.relationship: Questions the limits of Higham’s nativism framework and its economic-downturn explanation of restriction.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, appreciates the classic account while arguing that legislative triumph narratives can obscure categories produced after enactment. The 2024 article treats eugenics as one cause and argues that nativist surges accompany structural change even during expansion, rather than simply cyclical downturns. Benton-Cohen retains credit for the Dillingham finding. This does not certify every historical example or refute Higham's entire work; the original books remain unread.
